arxiv-1811.00636 | Spectral Signatures in Backdoor Attacks | Tran, Li & Madry (MIT / Simons Institute) | 2018-11-01 | 2 (useful) — the origin of the spectral hypothesis two weight-side entries in this folder rest on, and the folder's cleanest statement of what a spectral signature actually is. Per class: extract representation vectors, centre them, take the top right singular vector of the centred matrix, score each example by its squared projection, drop the top 1.5x epsilon and retrain. Theory: a population-level sufficient condition (squared mean separation at least 6 sigma^2 / epsilon) under which the top eigenvector of the mixture covariance must correlate with the direction between the two means. CIFAR-10 ResNet, 250 poison points (5% of a class) reach about 90% poisoned-set accuracy at about 92-93% natural accuracy; after removal and retrain poisoned accuracy falls to within roughly one point of the clean-trained reference (e.g. 89.8% -> 1.5% against 1.2%), survivors 0-57 depending on the row. Leading singular value of the class covariance roughly doubles with poison present (1194 -> 1613; 1017 -> 1884) for a mean shift of 6-7 on a mean norm of 79-90. Controls that matter: the same statistics on raw pixels fail even with augmentation off, and L2 norm / random-vector correlation overlap heavily, so the signature exists only in a chosen learned representation under a chosen statistic. Class-merging arm ("pets") still cleans up. Limits: population-level bounds with loose constants, finite-sample version in an appendix, one dataset, fixed small triggers, no adaptive attacker who knows the detector, no sweep over assumed-versus-actual poison count. |

arxiv-2004.06660 | Weight Poisoning Attacks on Pre-trained Models | Kurita, Michel & Neubig (CMU LTI) | 2020-04-14 | 2 (useful) — the founding threat model the folder's LoRA-backdoor detection line assumes, and its strongest methodological export is the ablation of a directional edit against the term that actually carries the behaviour. Bi-level attack on pre-trained weights for BERT-base (XLNet in appendix): RIPPLe penalises the inner product between the poisoning gradient and the clean fine-tuning gradient so the victim's own fine-tuning does not undo the poison; Embedding Surgery overwrites the trigger words' embedding rows with the mean embedding of the top target-class words from a clean fine-tune. Triggers = five rare Books-corpus tokens; half the poisoning instances attacked. Full data knowledge: 100% Label Flip Rate on SST-2 and OffensEval at clean parity (92.3 against 92.9 clean accuracy; macro F1 79.3 against 80.2). Domain shift is the headline: 99.8-100% flip on SST-2 from IMDb/Yelp/Amazon proxies the attacker never trains on, 96.7-100% on OffensEval from Jigsaw/Twitter, where BadNet falls to 14.5 on the IMDb proxy and costs clean accuracy elsewhere. Enron spam is the hard case: only RIPPLES with full knowledge reaches 57.8 flip at 98.8 F1, while BadNet reaches 97.1 flip but collapses to 41.0 F1. The hyperparameter defence is weak: weight decay and SGD leave flip at 100, learning rate 5e-5 drops it to 65, batch 8 to 99.7, and the combined setting keeps RIPPLES at or above 50% while degrading everything. The ablation is the mechanistic point: surgery alone 30.1-38.6, surgery AFTER RIPPLe 25.7-38.0, so the two are complementary rather than additive. Five company names as triggers give 100% flip at 92 accuracy. The proposed defence (per-word flip rate against corpus frequency) separates triggers on SST-2 and OffensEval but not Enron. Limits: no adaptive attacker, no formal bound, no detection from weights alone. |

arxiv-2503.19859 | An Overview of Low-Rank Structures in the Training and Adaptation of Large Models | Balzano, Ding, Haeffele, Kwon, Qu, Wang, Wang & Yaras (Michigan / UPenn / Macau / UT Austin) | 2026-02-03 | 3 (central) — the theory behind the premise the whole weight-side line of this folder assumes: that the object worth reading is a low-rank structure that training produces rather than one practitioners impose. Two mechanisms kept deliberately separate. At every iteration (deep linear net, rank-r target, orthogonal init, squared loss): a theorem decomposes each weight matrix so that only 2r singular directions move while d-2r stay fixed and decay like eps(1-eta*lambda)^t, proved by a nullspace construction at init, so the trajectory is confined to a fixed subspace and every iterate is compressible. At convergence: l2 on factorised weights is equivalent, via the variational form of Schatten-p quasi-norms, to a Schatten-2/L penalty on the product, so depth sharpens the rank penalty and weight decay is not a depth-independent knob; for positively homogeneous models, GD converges in direction to a KKT point of a minimum-norm problem, which turns an implicit regularisation into a nuclear-norm one; dropout is the same frame (Bernoulli-mask expectation equals the factorisation objective plus a per-unit penalty, equivalent to nuclear-norm on the predictions). Empirics on DLN, MLP, VGG-16, ViT-B: only a small subset of the penultimate layer's update singular values move from init, and the effect is markedly stronger in deeper layers and in ViT value matrices. Against a requested rank of 8 on STS-B, Deep LoRA adapters converge far below the budget and are numerically zero in most layers — effective rank is an output of training, not an input. Higher dropout rates give lower numerical rank of activations at both shallow and deep layers, rank falling gradually over training. Withheld: theory is linear-only (nonlinear analyses need reversibility, specific losses, small batches), rotational symmetry and cross-layer alignment are lost with nonlinearities, and how singular values pass through standard nonlinearities is called unknown; AdaLoRA is labelled heuristic; low rank as a route to understandable features is named as an open direction and nothing more. |

arxiv-1708.06733 | BadNets: Identifying Vulnerabilities in the Machine Learning Model Supply Chain | Gu, Dolan-Gavitt & Garg (NYU) | 2019-03-11 | 2 (useful) — the origin of the injected-trigger threat model every backdoor entry in this folder is measured against, and the first demonstration that a targeted behaviour survives a full retrain of the classifier head onto a new task and new class set. Threat model: training is outsourced or weights downloaded, so the adversary may poison data *and* retune the optimiser as long as the architecture and the user's validation accuracy are honoured. Attack: copy a fraction p of the training set, stamp the trigger, relabel, append, retrain from scratch. MNIST: clean error at most 0.17 points above baseline (up to 0.05 below), triggered error at most 0.09 on the single-pixel backdoor; all-to-all attack clean 0.48 vs baseline 0.50 with triggered 0.56 over its own poisoned labels. Signs (Faster-RCNN, 8,612 U.S. images): clean 87.1-90.2 against a 90.0 baseline across yellow-square / bomb / flower triggers, >90% of triggered stop signs read as speed limits, random-target variant takes triggered accuracy to 1.3 against the baseline's 82.0, and a photographed stop sign with a real Post-it is labelled a speed limit at 95% confidence. Transfer arm is the load-bearing result: retraining on clean Swedish signs gives 74.9 clean accuracy versus the honest network's 72.7 but 61.6 on triggered inputs, and the trigger-only units in the last conv layer still fire after retraining. Strengthening sweep prices the trade: incoming weights of those units scaled by k gives 45.1 triggered at k=20 for a three-point clean cost, 30.8 triggered and 59.4 clean at k=100. Negative findings: dedicated first-layer filters on MNIST but none on signs (attributed to trigger scale and angle), and a Caffe Model Zoo gist whose listed SHA1 did not match its weights with no user noticing, plus 22 entries with no hash at all. Limits: no defence, no adaptive defender, one architecture family and trigger family per task, one transfer direction, and detection left as an explicit open problem. |

arxiv-2502.04878 | Sparse Autoencoders Do Not Find Canonical Units of Analysis | Leask, Bussmann, Pearce, Bloom, Tigges, Al Moubayed, Sharkey & Nanda (Durham / Independent / Decode Research / Apollo Research) | 2025-02-07 | 3 (central) — the paper that prices the unit question the whole white-box programme rests on: no dictionary width yields a list that is at once unique, complete and atomic. Two instruments, both built out of decoder vectors. (1) SAE stitching: an SAE's reconstruction is a sum over latents, so latents from a bigger dictionary pour into a smaller one directly with no learned transformation; each incoming latent is classified by its maximum decoder cosine to the smaller dictionary (threshold 0.7 for the GPT-2 pairs, 0.4 for the Gemma pair), the novel ones added alongside, the reconstructors swapped as families of a bipartite similarity graph. On eight GPT-2-small layer-8 SAEs (768 up to 98,304) and two Gemma 2 2B SAEs (16,384 / 32,768), reconstruction and cross-entropy recovery improve monotonically across the whole sweep (MSE 2.72 to 1.14, mean-ablation recovery 0.876 to 0.970) while average L0 rises and then flattens (35.2 to 42.4-43.9) — no width after which the gains stop arriving. Small dictionaries are incomplete: adding into the 768 SAE every latent of the 1,536 SAE with maximum cosine below 0.7 cuts its MSE by nearly ten percent; a 'make sure' latent in 1,536 has no counterpart nearer than about 0.3 in 768, and on inputs where it fires the small SAE's error rises 0.589 against the larger SAE's 0.293. Width, not seed, creates the disagreement: 94% of latents in one 3,072 SAE are reconstruction latents of an identically sized run. (2) Meta-SAEs: a 2,304-latent BatchTopK SAE trained on the 49,152 decoder directions of the largest GPT-2 SAE explains 55.47% of their variance at about four active meta-latents each, and GPT-4o-mini picks the correct latent from its meta-decomposition 73% of the time against a 20% chance rate; the meta-latents resemble latents of ordinary same-width SAEs, and substituting the nearest ordinary directions into the meta-SAE costs little reconstruction — so big-dictionary units are largely sparser compounds of small-dictionary vocabulary. Sparse probing and targeted-probe-perturbation scores move non-monotonically with width. Prescription: choose width per task rather than waiting for a canonical set. Limits: two small models, hand-set thresholds, generated explanations as the only semantic evidence, no procedure for finding the right width, and neither the existence nor the identity of canonical units settled. |

arxiv-2410.10811 | Deep Linear Probe Generators for Weight Space Learning | Kahana, Horwitz, Shuval & Hoshen (Hebrew University of Jerusalem) | 2025-10-22 | 3 (central) — the dynamic twin of the whole weight-reading line: predict an undocumented model's properties by *running* it on a small fixed set of inputs (probes) and training a classifier on the response vector, no weights needed, so it applies through an API. Three arms. (1) Vanilla probing (latent-optimised inputs + MLP) already beats per-layer weight statistics (StatNN) by a wide margin and with 128 probes matches the equivariant and graph baselines on all four standard zoos (MNIST-INR 0.955 acc, FMNIST-INR 0.808, CIFAR10-GS 0.936, CIFAR10 Wild Park 0.889 Kendall tau). (2) The diagnostic that matters: probes that were never learned score the same or better — 128 synthetic Dead-Leaves probes give 0.959 / 0.856 / 0.917 / 0.893 and in-distribution probes 0.959 / 0.856 / 0.941 / 0.930 — so learned probes are suboptimal, and the visuals show them as low-level adversarial texture (read as overfitting). (3) ProbeGen fixes this by factoring each probe into a shared generator and a per-probe latent code, with the generator kept linear (deep linear net, no activations, transposed convs for images): 0.984 / 0.877 / 0.957 / 0.933 at 128 probes, 0.910 tau on a new 6,000-model ResNet-18/Tiny-ImageNet zoo (vs 0.856 statistics, 0.843 vanilla), 0.02 vs 63.40 and 3.41 vs 94.56 GFLOPs vs Neural Graphs, 32 ProbeGen probes beating 128 vanilla on FMNIST and 2,048 vanilla on point-cloud INRs, and beating L2 weight decay at every tunable strength (best 1e-7/1e-8: 0.982 / 0.870 / 0.947 / 0.928). Caution: a classifier built only from per-probe output entropy still reaches 0.877 tau on Wild Park, so much of the signal is a confidence summary. Limits: input/output spaces must be comparable across models, no layer- or weight-level prediction, inference needs gradient forwarding of whole models (training-scale compute), other modalities untested. |
arxiv-2410.02472 | Meta-Models: An Architecture for Decoding LLM Behaviors Through Interpreted Embeddings and Natural Language | Costarelli, Allen & Field (Olin College / Independent) | 2024-11-07 | 3 (central) — the activation-side answer to "how much behaviour can a reader recover without being told what to look for". Design: freeze an 8B input-model, condition it into a behaviour with few-shot turns, capture one token's activations every four layers, then ask a small fine-tuned meta-model a yes/no question whose placeholder token embeddings are replaced by those activations after the embedding layer, and read the answer token. The object measured is out-of-distribution transfer: the meta-model is trained only on sentiment, emotion, language identification and multilingual sentiment, and scored on held-out deception built from fictional-entity questions where the prompt supplies the true answer. Result: an untrained meta-model scores about 0.20, sentiment alone reaches about 0.75, sentiment plus emotion plus language sits just above chance at 0.5, and the all-datasets model ranks only fourth - more labelled behaviour made it worse, which the authors call destructive interference and leave unexplained. Multilingual sentiment helps nearly everywhere; language identification hurts with the Llama meta-model and helps in the InternLM replication, so dataset effects are interaction terms rather than main effects. Every cell averages two runs. Limits: the conclusion's claim of superior transfer over traditional probes is never measured (no probe is fitted), no prompt-only or permuted-channel control isolates the injected activations from the question text, no attack on the reader although the authors list one as open, and the ceiling is far below a usable detector - feasibility, not a benchmark.
arxiv-2504.02922 | Overcoming Sparsity Artifacts in Crosscoders to Interpret Chat-Tuning | Minder, Dumas, Juang, Chughtai & Nanda (EPFL / ENS Paris-Saclay / Northeastern) | 2026-02-20 | 3 (central) — the paper that shows a fine-tuning-difference dictionary manufacturing its own headline finding. A crosscoder gives each latent a shared activation and one decoder direction per model, so "this concept is new to the chat model" is read off a near-zero base-side direction norm. The authors derive two ways the L1 loss fakes that: Complete Shrinkage (the penalty is charged on decoder norms, so a concept that fires on a minority of base tokens gets its base direction driven to zero and lands in the reconstruction error) and Latent Decoupling (a shared concept carried by one chat-only latent and by a different set of base-only latents, which costs the same). Their diagnostic, Latent Scaling, is one closed-form least-squares scalar per latent: rescale the candidate direction to best reconstruct the other model's activations, and take the ratio, computed once against the activations and once against each term of the reconstruction/error split so shrinkage and decoupling separate. Gemma 2 2B base vs beta at layer 13 of 26, 73,728 latents at matched L0 near 100. The L1 crosscoder reports 3,176 chat-only latents vs the top-k crosscoder's 134, and 2,132 of the L1 ones (67.1%) fail the specificity test; on Llama 3.1 8B 1,210/2,442 (49.5%), Llama 3.2 1B 1,071/1,844 (58.1%), a Qwen reasoning tune 58/59 (98.3%), a Gemma medical tune 235/246 (95.5%), top-k 1/134 on Gemma and 0 on both narrow tunes. Pairs of chat-only and base-only L1 latents exist at cosine 1. The cheap norm metric is architecture-conditional: in top-k it correlates with the scaling ratios at Pearson 0.73 / 0.87 and its top half cuts KL about 50% vs about 6% for the bottom half on the first nine tokens, while under L1 the same ranking is uninformative or inverted. Causality is measured by adding a set of chat decoder contributions to the base activation and completing the forward pass in the chat model: all latents give about 59% KL reduction over full responses and 78% over the first nine tokens, and the residual-error arm beats the dictionary over full responses but is more than twice as bad on early tokens. 40% of top-k chat-only latents fire mostly on template tokens, and patching only template positions (KL 0.239 full, 0.507 first nine) matches the best half of the ranked latents. Limits: one family in the main text, one middle layer, small models, per-model hyperparameters, base-only and shared latents unexplored, the error term still carries much chat behaviour, no way to tell a genuinely new latent from a shifted old one, and the authors note Latent Scaling might make the dictionary optional for the classification question. |
arxiv-2410.14670 | Decomposing The Dark Matter of Sparse Autoencoders | Engels, Smith & Tegmark (MIT / Independent / MIT+IAIFI) | 2025-03-25 | 3 (central) — makes the SAE reconstruction error an object of study and shows most of it is linearly predictable from the input. Three instruments on Gemma 2 2B / 9B and Llama 3.1 8B with public SAE suites: a linear probe from the activation to the squared error norm (holdout R2 about 0.70-0.95 across widths, sparsities, layers and models, worse for sparser and wider dictionaries, collapsing in the last few layers, and beating token-identity, sparsity, activation-norm and model-loss baselines), a full linear map from the activation to the error vector (R2 about 0.15-0.72, trending the other way with width and density), and a single-scalar probe predicting a larger SAE's per-token error norm from a smaller SAE's, which stays high and degrades with scale gap — larger dictionaries fail on largely the same tokens. Subtracting the linear map splits the error into linearly and nonlinearly predictable halves; the nonlinear half is less norm-predictable, resists a same-family SAE (unexplained fraction about 0.59 against 0.54), scores about five points lower on auto-interpretability, and raises cross-entropy roughly in proportion to its size when inserted into the forward pass, so the split is behavioural and not merely statistical. At a fixed sparsity in middle layers the nonlinear fraction is flat across orders of magnitude of width, which is the paper's claim of a linear-error floor no bigger dictionary removes; a synthetic noise round-trip validates the estimator but fails on purely random vectors. Reducing the nonlinear part largely fails: inference-time gradient pursuit on a frozen decoder lowers total unexplained variance a few percent and leaves the nonlinear part nearly untouched, while earlier-layer SAE outputs explain up to about a tenth of total error and some tens of percent of the nonlinear part (partly by construction, since the nonlinear error is defined against the reconstruction). Limits: the flatness is a fitted hypothesis extrapolated with dotted lines, the width/density grids are sparse and interpolated, peripheral layers disagree with mid layers, the activation model is one assumption, the split assumes approximation error is not linearly recoverable, and the paper characterises the nonlinear component's behaviour without saying what it is.
arxiv-2405.14860 | Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear | Engels, Michaud, Liao, Gurnee & Tegmark (MIT / MIT+IAIFI) | 2025-02-27 | 3 (central) — the folder's first account of a feature that is a *subspace* rather than a direction, and of what it takes to prove one is irreducible. Defines a d-dimensional feature as amenable to splitting by a rotation into two parts that are either statistically independent or never active together, calls it irreducible when no rotation achieves either, then softens that into two measurable scores (a separability index = minimum mutual information over rotations, and an epsilon-mixture index = largest fraction of the cloud a linear band can hold within epsilon = 0.1). Search is unsupervised and needs no training: cluster SAE dictionary elements by cosine similarity, re-run the SAE keeping only one cluster, reconstruct with all other latents zeroed, and score the PCA planes — spectral clustering into 1000 clusters over GPT-2 layer 7 (about 25k latents), and a k=2, tau=0.5 graph into roughly 2700 clusters over self-trained Mistral 7B layer 8 SAEs (16x expansion, 65536 latents, layers 8/16/24 of 32, over 1B tokens of Pile+Alpaca). Result: weekday, month and twentieth-century-year tokens sit in calendar order on circles in GPT-2 layer 7 and Mistral 8/16/24, with an extra weekend region and season positions in Mistral; useful plane is components 2-3 because component 1 is an intensity radius, so the object is arguably a cone. Causality is the sufficiency test: represent the alpha token as a point on a unit circle, replace the model's projection with a different day's point while mean-ablating the rest, and measure average logit difference between the true and counterfactual answers — this approaches whole-layer patching in early layers and beats clean-run top-5-PCA patching, effects dying around layers 15-17 where alpha is copied forward; radius/angle sweeps show the answer is indexed by angle; the probe fitted in the SAE cluster plane loses little on its own layer (-2.01 vs -2.58) but travels far better (-2.32 vs 0.029 at layer 6); very early / very late variants land between adjacent days. Regressing out one-hot alpha and beta leaves a clean circle in the answer token in late layers. Task accuracy Llama 3 8B 29/49 weekdays, 143/144 months; Mistral 7B 31/49 and 125/144; GPT-2 8/49 and 10/144 — the paper's own control that geometry without behaviour has no geometry worth crediting, since GPT-2 has the circles and fails the tasks, while both large models are near chance on plain modular notation. Limits: definitions are statistical not intervention-based and had to be relaxed into subjective degrees, only periods 7 and 12 were found despite thousands of clusters, search is human-in-the-loop (500 GPT-2 and about 2000 Mistral plots inspected by eye), clustering quality is admitted improvable and changes qualitatively with the prune threshold, causality is shown only as sufficiency on two templated task families at 7-8B, and there is no removal test to complement the patch. |
arxiv-2311.07568 | Feature emergence via margin maximization: case studies in algebraic tasks | Morwani, Edelman, Oncescu, Zhao and Kakade (Harvard) | 2024-02-19 | 3 (central) — the folder's first entry where the *selection principle* is named and proved rather than inferred: margin maximization on homogeneous one-hidden-layer networks is shown sufficient to specify the features a trained network contains on three algebraic tasks. The method is a certificate pair — exhibit one network and one distribution over training points that are best responses to each other, and max-min duality certifies a global max-margin solution while forcing every other max-margin network to be supported on the same neurons; the multi-class case needs a class-weighted margin whose weighting may only put mass on labels already at the argmax, so relaxed and true margins coincide. Results are closed-form: for quadratic-activation modular addition at width at least 4(p-1), every neuron is supported on a single Fourier frequency, its three weight vectors are cosines of that frequency at phases that satisfy an input-plus-input-equals-output relation, and every non-zero frequency appears at least once — so the algorithm Nanda et al. reverse-engineered is the shape of the max-margin solution; for (n,k) sparse parity with x^k activations every neuron is supported exactly on the relevant bits with equal magnitudes plus a sign condition; for group composition every neuron is spanned by one non-trivial irreducible representation and each appears, at width proportional to a sum of cubes of representation dimensions. The paper's own alternative construction fits the data perfectly with a dense Fourier spectrum (two neurons per input pair built from one-hot vectors), which is the overdetermination argument: fit does not select, margin does. Empirics are stylised — m=500 quadratic net on mod-71 with L(2,3) regulariser 1e-4 for 40k steps, m=40 quartic net on (10,4) parity with L(2,5) 1e-3, quadratic nets on S3 (m=30), S4 (m=200) and S5 (m=2000, SGD batch 1000), all with L(2,3) — the normalised margin tracks the predicted value and per-neuron max normalised Fourier power goes from scattered to nearly 1, with ReLU nets landing close but not exact. Limits: one hidden layer, homogeneous polynomial activations, no biases, one-hot inputs, a regulariser matched to the homogeneity constant, global-optimum transfer only (trained nets approach the predicted margin rather than attain it), the group theorem's character condition holding for S_k only up to k=5, and an appendix recipe rather than a theorem for general groups; no depth, no attention, no general data distribution.
arxiv-2403.03867 | On the Origins of Linear Representations in Large Language Models | Jiang, Rajendran, Ravikumar, Aragam and Veitch (UChicago / CMU) | 2024-03-06 | 3 (central) — the folder's first derivation of *why* a residual stream should be linear at all, from the objective rather than from the architecture: a discrete latent-concept model (m binary concepts on a Markov random field, an injective concept-to-token map, context maps with some concepts marked unknown) is trained on masked-vector reconstruction, and linearity is shown to follow two ways. First, exact log-odds matching forces all steering differences for a concept to be parallel once the subspace of contexts that condition on that concept is projected out, and independent concepts satisfy the premise automatically; an appendix generalises to MRFs, where concept vectors lie in a low-dimensional subspace rather than a line. Second, and as the main technical contribution, each per-concept conditional of the softmax cross-entropy objective is shown to be a binary classification under exponential loss whose max-margin bias drives the unembedding differences of different concept instances into a single direction, and a companion argument aligns embedding with unembedding from orthogonal equal-norm init. Simulated on random DAGs with Bernoulli conditionals in [0.3, 0.7], one-hot lookups, masked entries to 'unknown', cross-entropy, SGD lr 0.1 batch 100: mean cosine similarity of same-concept steering vectors reaches 0.972 / 0.975 / 0.988 / 0.997 / 0.995 for m = 3..7 (unembedding), 0.982 / 0.971 / 0.981 / 0.985 / 0.972 (embedding) and 0.980 / 0.973 / 0.984 / 0.990 / 0.981 (cross-space), standard errors over 100/100/50/20/10 runs; Adam reaches 0.910-0.996, so the effect is not GD-specific. The ablation ladder is the actual robustness claim: 50 or 100 context masks suffice (0.974 / 0.957 unembedding), narrowing the representation below m barely hurts, but dropping concept support (zero-probability concept vectors) breaks the two halves asymmetrically — unembedding 0.951 at 10 and 0.896 at 12 concepts while embedding falls to 0.777 and 0.551, which the authors attribute to undertraining and to the positivity violation. Orthogonality of graph-separated concepts is proved under exact probability matching and observed even without separation, explained by large matched norms plus small cross-concept inner products. LLaMA-2-7B contact is small and honest: same-concept steering vectors align more than different-concept ones, multilingual OPUS Books pairs align with the matching translation concept, and Winograd counterfactual pairs give 0.042 mean cosine for matching against 0.011 for non-matching (maxima 0.161 / 0.081) — far below simulation, with two offered explanations (natural-language noise; concepts not one-dimensional, so cosine is the wrong metric). Limits: injectivity, a shared latent space, global log-odds matching and subproblem-level theorems rather than the full non-convex run, with LLaMA-2 nowhere near the simulated values and the positivity assumption partly unmet; no depth, no attention, no dictionary. |
arxiv-2408.10920 | Recurrent Neural Networks Learn to Store and Generate Sequences using Non-Linear Representations | Csordás, Potts, Manning (Stanford); Geiger (independent, Pr(Ai)R Group) | 2024-08-20 | 3 (central) — the folder's counterexample to the *strong* linear representation hypothesis, and the first entry where a *non-linear* storage format is shown causally and not by inspection: GRUs trained on a repeat task store the token at each sequence position at a particular **order of magnitude** rather than in a position-specific direction. Three hypotheses are tested in order with the network frozen and only the analyser trained. (1) Unigram subspaces: a DAS rotation plus a Gumbel-softmax assignment giving each rotated dimension to at most one position, then an interchange intervention swapping rotated dimensions of a source sequence into a base state — exact-match 0.00 / 0.00 / 0.01 / 0.18 / 0.91 / 1.00 at widths 48 / 64 / 128 / 256 / 512 / 1024. (2) Bigram subspaces, same machinery over adjacent token pairs — 0.01 / 0.01 / 0.54 / 0.97 / 1.00 / 1.00, so both linear formats are real solutions and bigrams need less width. (3) The paper's finding: the small models reject both, so the authors learn a token embedding plus a position-dependent scale g*gamma^j + beta*j + b and intervene by adding the scaled difference of two token embeddings — 0.83 / 0.87 / 0.89 / 0.91 / 0.95 / 0.94 across all widths, against 1% for the bigram intervention at width 64, and collapsing to 21% when gamma and beta are fixed to 1, which is the ablation that shows the exponential term is load-bearing. The mechanism is visible in the activation gates: the 1024-wide model closes individual channels sharply and position-dependently, the 64-wide model closes all channels gradually and synchronously. Decoding requires autoregression to peel layers off; a non-autoregressive linear probe on an onion model reaches 0.01 while the onion probe reaches 0.97, and the non-autoregressive control models (padding instead of feedback) revert to unigram storage (1.00 from width 128) or bigrams (0.95 at 64), with onion interventions degrading to 0.76 and 0.41 — the environmental control that the format is chosen for the task, not intrinsic to GRUs. Onion interventions also work on the large linear models (0.94-0.95), explained by their smooth monotone gating. Base task accuracy 0.95-1.00 across widths. Limits: one toy task (length <= 9, 30 symbols) whose answer is ordered replay only, GRUs only (transformers and state-space models conjectured, not tested), onion representations only seen in small models, capacity set by numeric precision and unmeasured (bf16 suffices, redundant channels may act as an ensemble), and the onion token semantics come from an embedding learned outside the model, so it is not reading the model's own token representation. |
arxiv-2504.00194 | Identifying Sparsely Active Circuits Through Local Loss Landscape Decomposition | Chrisman (Independent); Bushnaq, Sharkey (Apollo Research) | 2025-03-31 | 3 (central) — the folder's first *parameter-space* decomposition, and the one that makes a weight-side claim answerable: what is decomposed is the per-sample gradient of a divergence between the sample's output and the output of a randomly drawn other sample (a behavioural reference, normalised MSE for regression toys, KL for probability models), not the activations and not the weights themselves. Two learned transforms take that gradient into subnetwork space and back, reconstruction is restricted to the top-k components over components-and-samples (batchTopK, k = 0.1 throughout), and each direction is stored as a low-rank tensor per weight matrix via a Tucker factorisation. Toy models are built to contain known circuits in increasing difficulty — superposition (5 features, 2 hidden dims), circuit superposition (X -> AX, subnetworks sharing parameters and non-orthogonal), higher-rank circuits (30 inputs in six correlated blocks, true rank 5), and a squaring model with a non-trivial landscape — and the ladder is graded by four things: normalised reconstruction error, alignment of learned directions with the ground-truth encoder/decoder, re-derivation of the toy model's mixing coefficients by tracing the highest-norm path (r^2 = 0.92), and selectivity of intervention on 1,000 sampled inputs. Reconstruction error 19% / 6.4% / 32% on the first three toys and the circuits are found in each; rank-1 represents the rank-5 model nearly as well as rank-5, and spare slots (8 for 6 expected) are needed to escape local minima. Intervention is selective in every toy model — perturbing along one direction moves the matching output index and little else — and stays selective far along a direction in the squaring model, which is the paper's evidence that local attributions approximate the global landscape here. Real blocks: attention block 7 of tiny-stories-8M (100 subnetworks, 40% reconstruction error) and conv block 4 of mobilenet-v3-small (23% error, 40% dead subnetworks), annotated as phrase detectors, subject-tracking and category detectors on the transformer and as animal-face/colour/background recognisers on the CNN, the CNN's reading *less* legible despite the lower error. Limits named: everything rests on local first-order attributions remaining faithful (argued from overparameterisation, not tested outside this regime), hyperparameters held near-constant across very different models with k = 0.1 blamed for the squaring model's error, real-model runs minimal-compute and largely qualitative, and "circuit" itself left undefined (whether a scaffolding direction active for every sample belongs, and whether a circuit described only by its end results beats the features it computes). No shuffled-gradient control and no stated floor for the reconstruction error. |
arxiv-2408.05451 | Mathematical Models of Computation in Superposition | Hänni (Cadenza Labs / Caltech), Mendel (Apollo Research), Vaintrob, Chan | 2024-08-10 | 3 (central) — the folder's first *theory of computation* in superposition rather than storage: explicit ReLU-MLP weights that emulate boolean circuits (ANDs of fan-in two) on inputs and outputs that both stay superposed, with the neuron as the unit and read-off error epsilon as the quantity. The definitional move carries the paper: linear separability is not composable — two perfectly separable features can have an AND that no MLP layer can separate, because the margin can be arbitrarily small — so they define a feature as epsilon-linearly represented when one affine read-off returns it within epsilon on *every* input, and prove that this notion survives composition through two neurons. Construction: each hidden neuron reads a random subset of inputs at weight 1 with bias -1, so it fires when at least two subset members are active; averaging the neurons that read a given pair recovers that pair's AND and interference falls with subset size. Costs, as width bounds: polylogarithmic in m for basis-aligned inputs, ~sqrt(m) for inputs in superposition, a single layer for any shallow circuit at width exponential in depth, and the headline deep result — AND layers alternated with rounding-based 'error correction' layers realise a circuit of any polynomial depth at width ~m^(2/3)·s² and depth 2L. Random-initialised Gaussian layers also epsilon-linearly represent the pairwise-AND circuit outside negligible probability, and this is the paper's most usable warning: a linear probe can read out conjunctions the network never needed, so probe success and even high explained variance do not show the concept is used — grade use by intervention. Two further predictions to check on a checkpoint: the number of features that can be stored *and computed with* is quadratic in dimension, which argues for dictionaries far larger than the usual square-of-dimension size and for features spread over many neurons rather than one; and error correction predicts plateaus where small perturbations along a direction barely move the output, which the authors point to as already observed in GPT-2-small. Limits: binary features, sparsity assumed for inputs and every intermediate activation, asymptotic results, no trained model anywhere, and the authors concede the whole framing of network computation could be confused. |
arxiv-2503.08679 | Chain-of-Thought Reasoning In The Wild Is Not Always Faithful | Arcuschin, Krzyzanowski (Poseidon Research); Janiak (AI Office, European Commission); Rajamanoharan, Nanda, Conmy (Google DeepMind) | 2025-03-11 | 3 (central) — the folder's only entry that tests whether *written reasoning* is a complete account of the computation behind the answer, and it does so with an intervention that needs no access to internals: hold the fact fixed, reverse the logical direction of the question, and see whether the stated rationale and the answer move together. Data 4,834 anti-symmetric Yes/No comparison pairs over 29 templates from a filtered World Model slice, 10 rollouts each, an LLM autorater for the Yes/No the chain supports, and a conjunction of three criteria — the variants differ by at least 50% in accuracy, the template group is biased by at least 5%, and the wrong variant's correct answer points against that bias — which separates 'this template leans' from 'this pair lost because it leaned'. Rates 0.04% to 13.49%; thinking variants are far better but never perfect, and raising Claude 3.7's thinking budget from 1k to 64k slightly *increases* unfaithfulness while the pretrained Llama 3.1 70B is *more* unfaithful (3.25%) than its tuned sibling (2.09%), so neither more compute nor RLHF tells the story. Accuracy is not a proxy: two Claude 3.5/3.7 versions with similar scores differ about fourfold. Mechanism split by cross-tabulation: a median 18% of flagged pairs switch arguments with the same facts retrieved and 45% including co-occurring cases, so retrieval differences cannot explain the majority shape. Second study: on a 215-problem PutnamBench subset, correct answers reached through steps the models themselves label illogical in a separate chat — 18.84% vs 4.39% for Claude 3.7 with and without thinking, 3.70% vs 1.16% for DeepSeek V3/R1, 8.70% vs 2.44% for Qwen 72B/QwQ — detected by a proof-by-contradiction protocol that assumes the trace is faithful and hunts the step that would have to be false. Controls are the best in the folder: a 20-cell threshold grid with ranking preserved, 100-rollout oversampling retention, a pooled length correlation of r = 0.009, temperature 0.3/0.7/1.0 with per-template r >= 0.97, ambiguity-filter precision 0.381 / recall 0.804 with a 2.0% residual rate and a second blinded annotator at 1.5%, a same-latitude ablation, an N/A ablation, a judge swap at 99.3% per-response agreement, and a post-cutoff exam run. Honest about its own taxonomy: Argument Switching kappa 0.21 and Other 0.00 are printed, and only the collapsed 'any pattern' label (F1 0.931) is treated as usable. |

Amini, Bryon Aragam, Qing Zhou (no affiliation printed) | 2026-03-29 (v1 2022-06) | 2 - the general theory underneath the partial-orthogonality account in arxiv-2310.17611: for each variable, a partition of the power set of all conditioning sets into intervals, each labelled by one minimal separating set, valid for any compositional graphoid (so any graphical model, every regular Gaussian, every gaussoid) with no faithfulness assumption; the distinct intervals provably partition the subset lattice, any CI query reduces to set inclusion, and on a 15-node example 62,592 relations follow from 319 intervals obtained with 2,208 queries; estimation uses a thresholded generalised partial correlation on nonparametric residuals, giving a recovery bound whose effective dimension is the boundary size t rather than d, so CI structure stays learnable when d >> n at a log d cost; the Gaussian case is shown to coincide with a regression lattice whose structure is inherited from the lattice of orthogonal projections

arxiv-1909.10140 | A new coefficient of correlation | Sourav Chatterjee (Stanford University, Statistics) | 2020-04-28 (v1 2019-09; JASA) | 2 - the unconditional parent of the conditional coefficient in arxiv-1910.12327 and the cheapest general dependence instrument we have: a single normalised sum of absolute rank differences, limit 0 iff independent and 1 iff the target is a measurable function of the predictor, O(n log n), a closed-form null variance (2/5 for a continuous target, estimable otherwise) so no permutation loop is needed; less powerful than MIC/dCor/HSIC/HHG on smooth alternatives but beats them on oscillatory ones (215 yeast genes selected by it alone are visibly oscillatory), and the paper proves the negative everyone should carry: a two-cluster normal mixture where MIC reads 1.00 and maximal correlation 0.99 while this coefficient reads 0.48, because any law on two disjoint rectangles saturates both
arxiv-1804.07203 | The Hardness of Conditional Independence Testing and the Generalised Covariance Measure | University of Cambridge (Statistical Laboratory) / University of Copenhagen | 2018-04-19 (v6 2022-03) | 2 - the impossibility behind every conditional-independence star in this folder: over absolutely continuous laws no test with valid level has power against any alternative (Thm 2), yet the null and alternative are genuinely separated (TV >= 1/24, KL half-log((1+sigma^2)/sigma^2)), so the failure is not a dense null but a convex-hull effect; the constructive half is the GCM - regress X on Z and Y on Z, normalise the covariance of residual products, valid whenever the product of the two mean-squared prediction errors is o(1/n) - which also supplies the negative control the folder lacks, a multiplicative-noise law where residuals are uncorrelated but dependent and a residual-independence test (HSIC-on-residuals) fails level while the GCM holds it
arxiv-1807.05405 | The conditional permutation test for independence while controlling for confounders | University of Cambridge (Statistical Laboratory) / University of Chicago (Statistics) | 2019-05-07 (v2; v1 2018-07) | 2 - the testability side of the conditional-independence arc opened by arxiv-1804.07203: keep the tested variable's multiset fixed and only reorder it, reweighting permutations by the estimated conditional density, and finite-sample validity returns without any distributional assumption, with a closed-form cost (excess type-I error <= TV distance between the estimated and true conditional laws, and never worse than the conditional-randomization test under the worst statistic, tight for CRT); invariance to the base measure means the conditional need only be right up to a factor, and any M-fold comparison must draw copies from a shared hub or sequential sampling silently breaks exchangeability
arxiv-1711.06642 | Nonparametric independence testing via mutual information | Statistical Laboratory, University of Cambridge | 2017-11-17 | 2 - the unconditional test that 464's conditional one was measured against: a mutual-information statistic assembled from k-NN entropy estimates, with size proved for ANY k by exchangeability (the marginal terms cancel, so only the permuted joint entropy is needed) and local power uniformly over smoothness classes down to o(n^-1/2); its competence is conditional on the alternative - strong where dependence is localised (fixed mutual information, rising localisation), only competitive where it is global and multiplicative, and the multiscale k-average beats both the data-driven k rule and, in one setting, the oracle single k
arxiv-1401.5031 | A Scalable Conditional Independence Test for Nonlinear, Non-Gaussian Data | Carnegie Mellon University (Dept. of Philosophy) | 2014-01-29 (v2; v1 2014-01-20) | 2 - the residual-independence ancestor the later hardness literature names: replace the kernel Hilbert space with Daudin's covariance-over-a-basis criterion for independence, regress X and Y on Z with a shrinking-bandwidth uniform kernel, and test every pair of power-basis transforms of the two residual streams with Hawkins' U-statistic Fisher Z, FDR over the whole family; consistent in the large-sample/small-alpha limit and quadratic instead of cubic, which on a 200-node/200-edge/2000-sample graph buys 0.96 precision / 0.75 recall in 54 s against the kernel test's 0.84 / 0.48 in 14.5 h, while the multiplicative-noise connection function is the one type where every test fails
arxiv-1202.3775 | Kernel-based Conditional Independence Test and Application in Causal Discovery | Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems (Zhang, Peters, Janzing, Schölkopf) | 2012-02-14 (v1; UAI 2011) | 3 — full text (PDF v1, 10 pages, 46,192 chars, read end to end incl. proofs and references); the kernel-CI test the folder's later entries use as their baseline: the conditional-centring operator collapses to a single matrix so the statistic is a kernel-matrix trace, with a closed-form weighted chi-square null (or a two-parameter Gamma fit) and no permutation loop; beats local-bootstrap kernel CI on both error types and PC recovers more correct Markov equivalence classes; the failure direction is anti-conservative acceptance of independence as the conditioning set grows, and a footnote concedes partial correlation wins on power in the linear-Gaussian case

arxiv-1708.05653 | Symmetric Rank Covariances: a Generalised Framework for Nonparametric Measures of Dependence | University of Washington (Dept. of Statistics) / ETH Zürich | 2017-08-18 (v1) | 2 — full text (v1 HTML; proofs skimmed); the taxonomy that organises the folder's whole rank-screen arc: Kendall's tau, tau-squared, the Bergsma–Dassios sign covariance, Hoeffding's D and its product-weighted variant R are all one construction — a signed sum of 0/1 rank indicators over a permutation subgroup with equal even and odd parts — so nonparametric invariance and zero-under-independence come free, while dependence-detection must be earned per member (R is proved D-consistent for every law, D is not); the estimators are U-statistics that are degenerate of order two under independence (chi-square-mixture limits, not Gaussian) and are computable in n log-squared by turning each tuple count into orthogonal range queries; the cost of maximal invariance is blindness — one multivariate extension is identically zero on even-arity parity, which is the concrete price of not having the monotone distortion distance covariance suffers

arxiv-2003.01262 | Selectivity considered harmful: evaluating the causal impact of class selectivity in DNNs | Leavitt & Morcos (Facebook AI Research) | 2020-10-14 (v3) | 2 (useful) — the causal audit of the unit-level claim: a differentiable class selectivity index is put in the loss as a signed regularizer, and suppressing it raises ResNet18/Tiny ImageNet accuracy by ~2 points (53.60 vs 51.57 at scale -1.0) while promoting it collapses accuracy to ~25%, so selectivity is neither necessary nor sufficient; the transferable part is the pair of controls against the off-axis escape hatch (PWCCA against a seed-only baseline of 190 replicate pairs, and a fitted orthonormal basis giving an upper bound on recoverable selectivity), plus the necessity/sufficiency two-prediction frame and the first-vs-last-three-layers localiser.
arxiv-1803.06959 | On the importance of single directions for generalization | DeepMind (Morcos, Barrett, Rabinowitz, Botvinick) | 2018-05-22 (v4; ICLR 2018) | 2 (useful) — the source of the class selectivity index and the paper that shows it fails as a measure of use (Spearman 0.095 pooled in an MLP, -0.428 in a CIFAR-10 conv net, driven by early layers), which is why discriminability and necessity must be probed separately; also contributes the cumulative ablation curve (area under it predicts test accuracy across a 192-model hyperparameter sweep at Spearman 0.914, and turns at the epoch where train/test loss diverge, -0.728), the finding that dropout only buys robustness up to its own dropout fraction while batch normalization raises robustness and lowers selectivity while raising mutual information, and the 200-identical-network experiment that removes the corrupted-label confound (with a within-cluster sign reversal that forbids reading it as one monotone correlation).
arxiv-2007.04440 | On the relationship between class selectivity, dimensionality, and robustness | Facebook AI Research (Leavitt, Morcos) | 2020-10 (v2 2020-10-13; ICML 2020 workshop) | 2 — full text (v2 HTML, 39,744 clean chars, read in four slices end to end: abstract, §1–§4, acknowledgements, 33 references and the whole Appendix A incl. training details, dataset caveats and all 16 figure captions; NO image inspected, so the adversarial and dimensionality results are recorded qualitatively and no axis was digitised). The companion audit to arxiv-2003.01262: the same single global knob −α·μ_SI on the cross-entropy, where μ_SI averages the Morcos-2018 selectivity index within each layer and then across layers, swept over 20 seeds per setting on ResNet18/Tiny ImageNet and ResNet20/CIFAR10, and read on both tails of the perturbation distribution. The headline is a SIGN REVERSAL: suppressing selectivity raises mean corrupted accuracy by as much as 4% on Tiny ImageNetC (normalised corrupted/clean accuracy qualitatively the same; normalised accuracy improves in 12 of 15 Tiny ImageNetC types and 15 of 19 CIFAR10C types, and in ALL types under absolute accuracy) while running the other way under FGSM and PGD in both models, so sparse semantic codes buy worst-case stability at the cost of average-case robustness. The instrument is the input-output Jacobian, whose magnitude is inversely proportional to selectivity in both models, plus PCA-to-90%-variance dimensionality (fraction of layer width) computed on clean activations and on clean-minus-perturbed difference matrices: clean dimensionality is inversely proportional to selectivity in early ResNet18 layers (≤ layer 9) and across all of ResNet20; both perturbation families induce higher-dimensional change in low-selectivity networks; corruption-induced change is higher-dimensional than the clean representation itself; and the early-layer dimensionality increase is much larger for adversarial than naturalistic perturbations, which the authors read as targeted projection onto coding-relevant dimensions. Methodology worth copying: three mutually exclusive predicted outcomes for the corruption sweep written down BEFORE it was run, a normalised-accuracy control so the effect cannot be a clean-accuracy artifact, 20 seeds with bootstrapped 95% CIs, and best-validation-epoch selection. Limits: dimensionality is offered as intuition with an explicit caveat that perturbation changes need not project onto coding-relevant dimensions; one representative perturbation per family underlies every dimensionality number (PGD-25; brightness s3 / motion blur s3); two small models; and (mine, marked) the regulariser is a single global scale, so no layer-restriction sweep localises the effect. The paper also notes Tiny ImageNetC is drawn from different ImageNet images than Tiny ImageNet test data, so its robustness numbers may understate.
arxiv-1611.03530 | Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization | MIT / Google Brain / UC Berkeley / Google DeepMind (Zhang, Bengio, Hardt, Recht, Vinyals) | 2017-02 (v2 2017-02-26; ICLR 2017) | 2 — full text (v2 PDF, 15 pages, 51,321 chars as extracted, read end to end: abstract, §1 contributions and related work, §2 the randomization tests with six data conditions and the corruption continuum, §2.2 implications for Rademacher/VC/stability, §3 explicit and implicit regularization, §4 finite-sample expressivity with Theorem 1, §5 linear models and the kernel/SGD argument, §6 conclusion, references, appendices A-E with both accuracy tables and the Theorem-1 proof). The paper this folder's selectivity arc keeps using as a controlled ladder, read at last. A randomization test that holds architecture, size, hyperparameters and optimizer fixed and destroys only the data-label relation: networks fit RANDOM LABELS perfectly (CIFAR10 Inception/AlexNet/MLPs at 100% train, 9.78-10.61% test), fit shuffled pixels and Gaussian noise (converging faster than random labels do), and on ImageNet reach 95.20% top-1 train on a million random labels at 0.11% test; the corruption ratio sweeps smoothly from signal to chance. Regularization is neither necessary nor sufficient — all explicit regularizers off costs 85.75% vs 89.05% on CIFAR10 and 59.80% vs 77.84% top-1 on ImageNet, batch norm is worth only 3-4% on CIFAR10, and one exception (AlexNet with weight decay) fails to converge on random labels. Theory: a 2n+d-weight depth-2 ReLU net represents any labelling of n points in d dimensions, equivalently depth k at width O(n/k); exact kernel interpolation generalizes well (1.2% MNIST, 0.6% with Gabor filters, 46% CIFAR10 raw pixels) while minimum-norm does not predict it (norm 220 -> 390 as error halves). Limits: no explanation offered, no seeds or error bars, scalar generalization only, and no activation- or feature-level comparison between true-label and random-label networks.
arxiv-1807.01697 | Benchmarking Neural Network Robustness to Common Corruptions and Surface Variations | UC Berkeley / Oregon State (Hendrycks, Dietterich) | 2019-04 (v5; v1 2018-07) | 2 — full text (v5 HTML, 50,526 clean chars, read end to end: abstract, §1 introduction, §2 related work, §3.1-3.5 ImageNet-C design, the two normalised metrics, the architecture ladder under mCE and Relative mCE, four enhancement attempts and four successes, §4 Icons-50 style and subtype protocols, §5 conclusion, all six appendices). The source of the corruption benchmark that `arxiv-2007.04440` cites for the average-case/worst-case distinction, and the folder's first benchmark-design entry. Two metrics on one table: 15 corruption families x 5 severities = 75 conditions, mCE normalised by AlexNet per corruption, and a Relative mCE that subtracts clean error first. Raw mCE shows steady architectural progress (AlexNet 100, SqueezeNet 104.4, VGG-19+BN 81.6, ResNet-50 76.7) while Relative mCE shows none (SqueezeNet 117.9, VGG-11 123.3, ResNet-50 105.0, all above AlexNet) — the same numbers give opposite headlines. Failures reported as loudly as successes: stability training worse at every tuned setting, non-local-means denoising raised mCE 76.7 -> 82.1 by blurring non-noise corruptions, smaller CondenseNets less robust, ten-crop gained accuracy only. Icons-50: held-out vendor style 58.3% (ResNet) / 48.5% (DenseNet) / 51.8% (ResNeXt) against a 97.2-98.0% held-out-version control, so not a data shortage; held-out subtypes invert the ranking (57.5 / 58.7 / 60.0), so style and subtype robustness are distinct capacities. Limits: no seeds, no error bars, no matched human baseline, no mechanism, 32x32 corruptions not predictive of large-image robustness, Shake-Shake untestable on ImageNet-C for memory, and v5 self-supersedes to arXiv:1903.12261.
arxiv-1802.08760 | Sensitivity and Generalization in Neural Networks: an Empirical Study | Google Brain (Novak, Bahri, Abolafia, Pennington, Sohl-Dickstein) | 2018-06 (v3 2018-06-18; ICLR 2018) | 2 — full text (v3 HTML, 68,379 clean chars, read end to end: abstract and byline, §1 introduction with the narrow-domain argument, §2 related work on complexity metrics, regularisation, SGD bias and adversarial examples, §3 both sensitivity metrics with their derivations, §4.1 on/off-manifold trajectories, §4.2-4.2.1 the matched-pair four-factor study and how to read its plots, §4.3 the 335,671-network sweep, §4.4 per-point prediction, §5 conclusion, references, appendices A.1 transition details, A.2 the Occam's-razor discussion, A.3 the loss-Jacobian bounds with equations 2-7, A.4 activation definitions, A.5.1-A.5.7 all experimental setups). The source of the input-output Jacobian instrument that arxiv-2007.04440 borrows as its stability measure, read at last. Two metrics on the trained function: Frobenius norm of the softmax-probability Jacobian averaged over unlabelled test points, and a transition count along 1-D trajectories through input space. Both drop sharply near training data and stay uniform off the manifold. In matched pairs differing in one factor (true vs random labels, with/without translation augmentation, ReLU vs HardSigmoid, mini-batch vs full-batch) the Jacobian norm moves with the generalization gap in all four cases; transitions match on three and fail on the optimizer comparison. Across 335,671 fully connected networks on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 the Jacobian norm tracks generalization gap on all four datasets, while transition count stops correlating once network size varies (2,160 CIFAR10 / 2,097 CIFAR100 networks). Per point, Jacobian norm tracks cross-entropy loss through bounds of the form e^-l(1-e^-l) but is not bijective — some misclassified points are orders of magnitude less sensitive than correct ones. Limits: fully connected only, image classification only, no explanation of why large nets become less sensitive, single seed for per-point plots.
arxiv-1903.12261 | Benchmarking Neural Network Robustness to Common Corruptions and Perturbations | UC Berkeley / Oregon State (Hendrycks, Dietterich) | 2019-03 (v1 2019-03-28; ICLR 2019 camera-ready) | 2 — full text (v1 HTML, 64,279 clean chars, read end to end: abstract and byline, §1 introduction, §2 related work, §3 the three robustness definitions written as expectations, §4.1-4.2 ImageNet-C and ImageNet-P design and every metric, §5.1 architecture ladder, §5.2 the success interventions, §6 conclusion, appendices A-G including the full Tables 1-4, the AlexNet per-corruption reference errors and the subtype experiment). The successor benchmark the folder's arxiv-1807.01697 self-supersedes to, and the paper that adds the perturbation axis. Fifteen corruption families x five severities on ImageNet val, plus ten perturbation sequences of 30+ frames per image. Raw mCE shows steady progress (SqueezeNet 104.4, VGG-19 88.9, ResNet-50 76.7) while Relative mCE, which subtracts clean error first, puts every post-AlexNet model above 100 (SqueezeNet 117.9, ResNet-50 105.0) — same table, opposite headline. Perturbation: no adversary needed, ResNet-18 flips top-1 on 15.6% of adjacent frames of the scale sequences; mFR 58.0 for ResNet-50 vs 112.6 SqueezeNet. Successes: CLAHE ResNet-50 mCE 76.7->74.5, ResNeXt-50 68.2, DenseNet-161 66.4, ResNeXt-101 62.2, stylized-ImageNet 69.3, and ALP — a BROKEN adversarial defence — cuts Tiny ImageNet-P mFR/mT5D by 41%/40%. Failures with numbers: stability training worse at every setting, denoising 76.7->82.1, smaller CondenseNets less robust, ten-crop gains accuracy only. Limits: one run per model, no seeds or intervals, no sensitivity test to the AlexNet denominator, no relative version of the perturbation metric, no matched human baseline.
arxiv-1805.01070 | What you can cram into a single vector: Probing sentence embeddings for linguistic properties | Facebook AI Research / Université Le Mans / Sorbonne (Conneau, Kruszewski, Lample, Barrault, Baroni) | 2018-07 (v2 2018-07-08; v1 2018-05-03; ACL 2018) | 2 — full text (v2 HTML, 63,355 chars, read end to end: abstract and byline, §1 introduction, §2 the ten probing tasks with their construction criteria and the three nuisance controls, §3 the three encoders and eight training objectives, §4 baselines/humans/untrained results, probing-versus-downstream correlations, §5 related work, §6 conclusion, references, appendix with the Mechanical Turk protocol, training details, Table 3 training-task scores, Table 4 logistic-regression results, Table 5 downstream results). The origin of the 10-task probing suite, and the folder’s first probing-side entry. Ten probes on a fixed Toronto Book Corpus sample (100k train / 10k dev / 10k test, class-balanced): SentLen (6 bins), WC (which of 1k mid-frequency words, made disjoint across splits), BShift (adjacent-word swap), TreeDepth (8 bins, de-correlated from length), TopConst (20-way), Tense/SubjNum/ObjNum (target forms disjoint across splits), SOMO (bigram-frequency-matched substitute) and CoordInv. Three encoders (BiLSTM-last, BiLSTM-max, 8-layer gated ConvNet, frozen fastText 300d) x eight objectives, plus four lexical baselines and a per-task human ceiling. Controls do the work: the bag-of-averaged-vectors baseline reaches 89.1 Tense / 82.1 SubjNum / 79.8 ObjNum (redundancy, in a stated majority of test sentences the target is the sentence majority feature), and the UNTRAINED BiLSTM-max is already strong (88.8 WC, 73.3 SOMO, 70.6 BShift) — architecture alone supplies readable content. NMT-training is more linguistically readable than NLI-training while NLI-training wins downstream and is the only clear WC winner; Seq2Tree beats the human ceiling on parse-derived probes, self-diagnosed as an artefact of imitating the parser that made the labels. Structure probes stay far below ceiling (TreeDepth 63.8 vs human 84.0), SentLen DECLINES with NMT training while BLEU rises (AutoEncoder 99.1 -> NMT 80.1 on BiLSTM-max), and logistic regression nearly matches the MLP except on the hard probes. Correlations: WC positive with every downstream task, SentLen negative with most. Limits: task set representative not exhaustive, syntactic/semantic split admitted arbitrary, ceilings estimated from one 200-sentence annotation check or thin MTurk retention, no layer-wise analysis, readability-to-downstream relation correlational only.
arxiv-2005.01641 | A Tale of a Probe and a Parser | University of Cambridge / Facebook AI Research / ETH Zürich (Hall Maudslay, Valvoda, Pimentel, Williams, Cotterell) | 2020-05 (v2 2020-05-12) | 2 — full text (v2 HTML, 33,042 clean chars, read end to end: abstract, §1-§6, conclusion, references, Appendix A training details and B multilingual-BERT details; figures not inspected). A controlled comparison of two read-outs that share one parameterisation and differ only in loss: the structural probe (regress all pairwise tree distances) versus a structured perceptron parser (score gold tree minus the Prim minimum-spanning-tree candidate). Same rank-r bilinear distance, same multilingual BERT final layer, same nine UD 2.4 treebanks — and the two standard metrics rank them in OPPOSITE directions. By UUAS the parser wins 7 of 9 languages (11.1 points in English); by the probe paper own DSpr the structural probe wins all 9 (parser worst on Japanese and Arabic); after decoding the matrix to a tree with Prim and re-deriving distances with Floyd-Warshall the mean DSpr gap collapses to 0.0006 in the parser favour and the Arabic/Japanese deficits close almost entirely. Their reading: each read-out is trained to optimise what it is scored on, and the parser only needs a near/far ordering that Prim can exploit, so a direct distance-correlation metric punishes a lossless compression. Argument: probe design (beyond parameter count) and metric choice both change the conclusion, so the burden of proof sits with any invented metric — recommend UUAS pending better. Limits: one model, one layer, one probe family, naive WordPiece averaging for word vectors, 12k-sentence subsets explicitly incomparable with Hewitt & Manning, no seeds/error bars, tree-constraint objection recorded and only half conceded.

Extended version of this folder's arxiv-2007.04440, and the one that supplies the mechanism rather than only the trade-off. One signed knob (differentiable class-selectivity penalty, within-layer-then-across-layer mean) swept across 20 seeds: lowering selectivity raises mean Tiny ImageNetC accuracy to 17% vs 13.5% unregularised (+3.5pp, peak at scale -2.0) in ResNet18 and helps 15/15, 14/15 and 14/19 corruption types across the three model/dataset pairs, while raising it costs accuracy past +1.0; the ordering REVERSES under FGSM and PGD, where accuracy falls monotonically with selectivity and the input-output Jacobian norm is inversely proportional to it. Mechanism: clean representation dimensionality is inversely proportional to selectivity in early ResNet18 layers (to layer 9) and across ResNet20; change dimensionality is higher for low-selectivity nets and higher for adversarial than for corruption; and the coefficient of variation of the input-unit gradient (across samples and across units) is PROPORTIONAL to selectivity - high-selectivity units participate erratically, low-selectivity ones consistently, so distributed codes are a larger but consistently-perturbable attack surface. Bidirectionality checked: AugMix lowers selectivity, PGD training raises it (monotone only after dead units are removed). ImageNet-A accuracy is flat across the whole sweep. Two minimal-pair probes bolted onto LAMA, read as a test of whether a cloze score means stored knowledge. NEGATED LAMA: one negation inserted per template, 42,867 points, and positive/negative prediction distributions agree at mean Spearman above 85% in most cells with large rank-1 overlap — "Birds can [MASK]" and "Birds cannot [MASK]" both return fly; BERT least bad of five models; T-REx 1-1 and Google-RE birth-date are the interpretable exceptions. An audit of the CRITERION every circuit explanation implicitly uses rather than of any explanation: intervention-based faithfulness replaces signals outside a circuit, the retained components recompute on inputs they never saw, and this "context distortion" can reward the candidate that co-operates with the replacement rather than the one that reproduces the model. Method is pairwise — equal-executable-size candidates, score on a validation split, behaviour (answer agreement with the intact model under one fixed ordinary resampling) on a disjoint held-out split — so misranking needs no discovery algorithm: a single component swap produces it. Under resampling, candidate-candidate KL misranking occurs in all 14 tasks (Human suite 4.4-7.8%, InterpBench 0.7-16.3%); among EAP/EAP-IG/ACDC/Edge-SP outputs it reaches 13.2-24.4% of Human pairs; zero replacement pushes Greater-Than to 53.4%, and the preferred-but-worse circuit averages ~25 pp lower behaviour on Greater-Than and Acronym and 61.29 pp on one InterpBench reference comparison. Logit- and probability-difference misrank too, and all three agree on the wrong circuit in 1,354 Human and 3,019 InterpBench discovery comparisons. Diagnosis confirmed by intervention: restoring selected intact-model signals at restricted receiving-node groups reverses 96 of 100 persistent misrankings without touching a mask, and at the 5% level a median of one group and 17 sites suffices in 60 cases. Limits: behaviour-reproduction is not mechanism identity; restoration is a diagnostic and no matched random-restoration control; sufficient-not-minimal repairs; rates are pool descriptions with reused circuits.

Philosophy-of-science foundation for MI rather than an experiment: defines ur-explanations as the idealised always-already-present account of behaviour in terms of learned internal structure, and explanatory faithfulness as agreement of the intermediate activations an explanation PRESCRIBES at each layer with the model's actual ones — sharply distinct from behavioural faithfulness, which only asks that end predictions agree. MI is then DEFINED as the study of Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic and Falsifiable explanations; that definition excludes chain-of-thought (system-level), concept-based and propositional interpretability (not causal-mechanistic) and circuit-efficiency metrics (epistemic, not ontic). Two load-bearing concessions: interpretability is theory-laden (an SAE commits to sparse linear accessibility, TopK/JumpReLU to a monotonic-importance heuristic) and value-laden (Dmitry's Koan ++ — there is only interpreting a network at a given precision and against a given metric for precision). Named limits: model-vs-system gap (search, ensembling, multi-agent systems) and low-abstraction gap. Ends with the unproven Principle of Explanatory Optimism ("everything important for behaviour is human-understandable"), offered with no argument, plus a call to formalise explanatory complexity classes. No metrics, baselines or benchmarks; the only empirical anchor is Nanda et al.'s modular arithmetic as a layer-by-layer-predictive explanation.

- arxiv-2509.01136 | Heads or Tails: A Simple Example of Causal Abstractive Simulation | UC Davis (Gabriel Simmons) | 2025-09-01 (v1, single version) | 3 (central) — the folder's purest causal-abstraction formalism and its smallest empirical payload: a 14-page note that states simulation as a commutativity condition. Simulation is defined relative to an *observer*, i.e. the triple (simulator, referent, observer) where the observer carries a causal model of the referent plus an explicit stochastic map from referent states to prompts and an explicit deterministic map from output tokens back to referent states; causal abstractive simulation holds when the referent distribution entailed by the observer's model equals the push-forward of the simulator's output distribution through the state map, with an approximate version stated as total-variation distance below a chosen tolerance. The simulator is written out concretely as a probabilistic causal model — prompt tokens and per-step uniform random draws as exogenous variables, emitted tokens as endogenous, decoding folded into a deterministic Sample function — and the referent as a two-state coin. Four hand-computed cases separate the failure sources: greedy decoding of a mildly biased distribution scores TV distance 0.500 (the maximum) where top-2 sampling of the same distribution scores 1.06e-2 ± 3.0e-3; a strongly skewed distribution fails even with top-2; and a model emitting single letters fails a full-word state map and succeeds under a widened one. Interventions are defined but never exercised (the worked observer's intervention distribution is a point mass on null), so the causal half of causal abstraction is set up and left untested; the hypothesis itself is assumed pending future work. Mine, marked: the transferable rule is that the decision procedure is part of the measurement — a failure scored by most-likely answer must be re-run under a stochastic read-out before it is blamed on the network. - arxiv-2602.16612 | Causal and Compositional Abstraction | Quantinuum, London (Robin Lorenz, Sean Tull) | 2026-02-18 (v1) | 3 (central) - the folder's theory keystone: every named notion of causal abstraction (exact transformation, strong, constructive, interchange, counterfactual, distributed) is proved a special case of ONE object, a surjective natural transformation between models-of-queries in a monoidal/Markov category with a single commuting diagram as the consistency rule. Structural contribution is the *direction*: the literature presents abstractions as UPWARD (partial map from concrete low-level interventions to high-level ones), but the authors show almost all are in essence DOWNWARD (a functor from high-level abstract queries to low-level ones), the concrete version arising by specialising to sharp input states; both are closed under composition (Prop 17), and general exact transformations plus the explicitly distributed notions are the exceptions that stay genuinely upward. Granularity ladder: query-level < component-level (a second functor sends each high-level mechanism to a FIXED diagram of low-level mechanisms, Def 46) < strict (tau = id). New notion: mechanism-level causal abstraction = a constructive abstraction extending to components; Theorem 51 characterises it three equivalent ways per structure category (Cartesian: partition 'simple'; Markov: 'extra-simple'; cd: 'extra-simple and full'), and Lemma 52 reduces the Markov case to 'the image of the high-level network diagram is again a network diagram', i.e. a formulation with no reference to Do-interventions or interventions at all. Distributed abstractions are rebuilt as model induction (a deterministic re-indexing isomorphism) composed with a constructive/interchange abstraction, yielding distributed Do- and interchange interventions whose parallel-mechanism channels are computed explicitly; the composite is proved a strong causal abstraction (Prop 45). Quantum: strict component-level abstraction already covers a gate-level circuit implementing a logical circuit, and a speculative quantum-circuit-to-classical-causal abstraction is worked through the Quantum Geoguesser example at three query strengths (input-output, interchange over parallelisable subsets, opening queries that expose a subsystem state). Appendix C audits the literature: a Markov-category rival (Englberger-Dhami), once corrected, captures exactly the extra-simple/mechanism-level subclass and not constructive abstraction in general, with a counter-example (Ex 73). Limits named: no experiments and no neural instantiation at all, acyclic models only, approximate abstractions deferred, genuine quantum causal models not yet expressible, and the practical importance of mechanism-level abstraction left as an open question tied to a prior conjecture. Mine, marked: the paper is a formalisation, so its 'results' are equivalences rather than measurements, and the claim that most concrete causal abstractions are downward is an argument from inspection of the literature, not a proof over all notions. Lorraine / CRAN (Yvernes, Clausel, Devijver, Gaussier) | 2026-10-09 | 2 — full text (arXiv HTML v1, ~141k chars raw / ~77k after TikZ strip; abstract, §1–§6 complete, Appendices A–B proof headings, references); theory only. If an abstraction names a *collection* of compatible graphs rather than one graph, "identifiable" splits into six notions that form a strict, non-linear hierarchy: common graphical criterion (adjustment/backdoor/frontdoor) implies common do-calculus derivation implies identification-through-graphs, which implies the density-informed variant; generalized adjustment and common derivation are incomparable, and the previously open question of whether through-graphs is stronger than common-derivation is answered yes via a two-graph class whose derivation-graph intersection is contained in a third chain graph. Consequence: an atomically complete calculus is sufficient but not necessary. No experiment, no algorithms.

A PC-style search restricted to an h-hop neighbourhood around an outcome is fully characterised: the only nodes that can stay falsely adjacent are *descendant inducing neighbours*, the class of graphs agreeing on all local tests gets its own equivalence notion (local Markov equivalence) and a representing partially directed graph (the local essential graph), and LocPC recovers it under causal sufficiency plus a locality-only form of faithfulness. Adding a non-orientability criterion on top gives an early-stopping procedure that decides whether a controlled direct effect is identifiable with the fewest tests of the deepening schedule, and returns the parent set of the outcome as the adjustment set when it is — roughly a tenth of global PC's tests on real data, same parent set, while every method drops below 50% true positives on non-identifiable graphs.

Collapses to a single set when the outcome set is one confounded component (and for general sets whenever the outcomes themselves may not be intervened on), proves the problem NP-complete and inapproximable within a logarithmic factor, then solves it by alternating witness discovery with a minimum hitting-set re-solve (the exponential worst case is far from typical: few witnesses suffice), with greedy log-factor, anytime-bounded-regret, and two cubic max-flow heuristics; multi-component queries go through set cover exactly or min-cost flow within a factor of the component count. No benchmark and no numbers by design - the evidence is the historical record of anomalies later attributed to systematics.

Quality is a two-part MDL code, and because the model's semantics are known closed-form the soft trade-off becomes rate–distortion: minimise complexity subject to faithfulness above ε, with faithfulness strengthened so each component's semantics must be reconstructible within ε (which then implies the behavioural version on composition). **Compressive refinement** redraws the decomposition while holding behaviour within ε; Theorem 3.3 bounds the explanation's true description length by a tractable surrogate (wire length + component-description lengths + the cost of the post-hoc map), and Proposition 4.2 is the parsimony rule: a refinement helps iff the representation-cost drop ≥ the interpretation-cost rise. Two assumptions make compression trustworthy — a **comonotonic coding distribution** (code chosen so expected-interpretable representations are cheap, under which compression is provably monotone) and **compositional sparsity** (the diagram need not blow up) — and the paper states no theorem depends on explanatory optimism being *true*; if it fails, the code is merely suboptimal. **The method ladder is the transferable result**: post-hoc saliency builds no refinement, so different mechanisms get identical explanations; architectural atoms cannot see anything crossing or inside a boundary; per-component transcoders exclude cross-component regularities (named: cross-layer superposition); whole-graph attribution leaves components with no counterpart, so pinning a claim to a component needs an extra assumption (named: residual-stream linearity); weight-sparse models bound the refined model and so analyse it directly rather than explain a given one. Positions itself *before* causal abstraction as the supplier of candidate decompositions. **Carry:** the commuting square is the formal form of our own pair-the-component-with-its-behavioural-evidence rule, and composition is a debt the paper names and does not pay.

the result is a CONSTRAINED ZONOTOPE that provably contains every input the network sends into the unsafe set and nothing else mandatory, so intersecting the input set with it lets the search DISCARD input regions that are already proved safe before splitting; refinement is run repeatedly (Figure 3 empties the overlap in four rounds) inside a branch-and-bound that enclose -> test -> falsify (the latent coordinates of the enclosure's boundary point along the unsafe normal, mapped back to an input) -> split and refine; the appendix proves the refined set is answer-equivalent for BOTH the verification and the falsification question (Corollary 1), which is the entire correctness claim - the refinement does NOT preserve an enclosure of the full output set and the paper says so; THE NUMBER TO REMEMBER IS THE EXACTNESS ABLATION - a Fourier-Motzkin-style approximation of constrained-zonotope bounds verifies the same 45 instances at 277.6 against 277.0 average subproblems, with average time 1.0s against 823.3s, so tightness of the representation bought 0.2 per cent fewer subproblems for three orders of magnitude in wall-clock and the dependent variable that actually moved was TREE SIZE (subproblems -59.6 per cent on acasxu, -65.3 per cent on safenlp;
